passages.t: David called to war, and a silent heaven
passages.happening:
The Philistines gather their forces against Israel, and Achish tells David that he and his men must go out to battle with him (verse 1). David answers, “Then you will come to know what your servant can do.” Achish makes him his bodyguard for life (verse 2).

“Now by this time Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned for him and buried him in Ramah, his own city. And Saul had removed the mediums and spiritists from the land” (verse 3).

The Philistines camp at Shunem, and Saul gathers Israel at Gilboa (verse 4). ‘When Saul saw the Philistine army, he was afraid and trembled violently’ (verse 5). ‘He inquired of the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him by dreams or Urim or prophets’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The book has been moving toward this night since Samuel first told Saul that the LORD had rejected him. Samuel has died, and the narrator says so again here, to remind the reader that the prophet who guided and rebuked Saul is gone. The Philistines are about to fight the deciding battle, and David, strangely, is marching with them.

The armies have moved north. The Philistines camp at Shunem on the north side of the Jezreel Valley, and Saul on Mount Gilboa to the south. Holding that broad valley meant holding the main roads through the land.

The note that Saul had removed the mediums reflects the law of Moses, which forbade consulting the dead. Saul had once enforced it. That makes his visit tonight all the darker.

This is a law for Israel about its own worship. It gives no one today a reason to harm, threaten or shun any person. The note on Exodus 22:18 tells how verses about sorcery were misused in the witch trials of later centuries.

The LORD's usual ways of answering were dreams, the Urim kept with the priest's ephod, and prophets. Saul had cut himself off from the priesthood by killing the priests of Nob, and the one surviving priest, with the ephod, is with David. Samuel is dead. Saul asks, and hears nothing.
passages.later: The law forbade what Saul is about to do: “You must not turn to mediums or spiritists; do not seek them out, or you will be defiled by them. I am the LORD your God” (Leviticus 19:31), and it listed among forbidden practices anyone who ‘consults a medium or spiritist, or inquires of the dead’ (Deuteronomy 18:11).
passages.asks: Saul once drove the mediums out, and now he is afraid. Ask what convictions you hold firmly when life is calm, and what fear might tempt you to let go. And ask how you have responded when God seemed silent.

passages.happening:
Saul tells his servants, “Find me a woman who is a medium, so I can go and consult her.” There is one at Endor, they say (verse 7). Saul disguises himself and goes by night with two men. “Consult a spirit for me. Bring up for me the one I name” (verse 8).

The woman is afraid. Saul has killed the mediums and spiritists in the land, she says. ‘Why have you set a trap to get me killed?’ (verse 9). Saul swears to her by the LORD that no punishment will come to her (verse 10). “Whom shall I bring up for you?” the woman asked. “Bring up Samuel,” he replied (verse 11).

When the woman sees Samuel, she cries out, and she knows the king. “Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!” (verse 12). He tells her not to be afraid. She sees ‘a god coming up out of the earth’ (verse 13), an old man wrapped in a robe. ‘So Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed facedown in reverence’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Calling up the dead to learn the future was widespread in the ancient world. Texts from Mesopotamia and the Hittites describe rites for summoning spirits, sometimes through a pit dug in the ground, and some scholars connect the Hebrew word for medium with such a pit. Israel's law banned it because it sought guidance from some source other than the LORD and treated the dead as powers to be consulted.

Endor lies north of Shunem, near the hill of Moreh and Mount Tabor. To reach it, Saul had to slip round or behind the Philistine army, a dangerous trip made at night and in disguise.

There are reversals everywhere. Saul swears by the LORD to protect a practice the LORD forbade. The king who banned mediums is now asking one for help.

The woman calls what she sees by the ordinary word for God or gods, elohim. It could also be used of a being from beyond the world of the living. Samuel is known by his robe, the prophet's robe that tore in Saul's hand when Samuel said the kingdom would be torn from him.
passages.later: Isaiah asked the question the law implies: “When men tell you to consult the spirits of the dead and the spiritists who whisper and mutter, shouldn’t a people consult their God instead? Why consult the dead on behalf of the living?” (Isaiah 8:19).
passages.hard:
Did Samuel really come back from the dead at a medium's call?

Interpreters have given three main answers. Many, ancient and modern, hold that God really allowed Samuel to appear. They note that the narrator calls the figure Samuel, that his words come true, and that the woman herself seems shocked, as if something happened that she did not expect or control. The Jewish book of Ben Sira says that Samuel prophesied even after his death (Sirach 46). Others, among them a number of early Christian writers, argued that a deceiving spirit took Samuel's form, since God would not honor a forbidden practice. A third view sees the whole scene as the medium's own performance, though it struggles to explain the true prophecy.

Early Christian opinion was divided, and the text does not explain how it happened. These notes take no side.

What the chapter makes plain is that the practice is condemned, that the meeting brings Saul no help, and that God's word through Samuel stands. The chapter gives no support to seeking contact with the dead.
passages.asks: Saul went to a medium because God was silent. Ask where you look for guidance when God seems silent, and whether it draws you nearer to him or further away. And ask what it would mean to wait for God's word instead of forcing an answer.

passages.t: Samuel's last word, and a last meal
passages.happening:
“Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?” Samuel asks. Saul answers that he is deeply distressed. The Philistines are fighting against him, and “God has turned away from me. He no longer answers me, either by prophets or by dreams. So I have called on you to tell me what to do” (verse 15).

Samuel asks why he consults him, since the LORD has turned from him (verse 16). The LORD has done what he said: he has torn the kingdom out of Saul's hand and given it to David (verse 17), because Saul did not obey the LORD against Amalek (verse 18). The LORD will give Israel into the hand of the Philistines, ‘and tomorrow you and your sons will be with me’ (verse 19).

‘Immediately Saul fell flat on the ground, terrified by the words of Samuel’ (verse 20). He has eaten nothing all day and night.

The woman sees how shaken he is. She has risked her life to obey him, she says. Now let him listen to her and eat, so that he will have strength to go on his way (verses 21-22). He refuses, but his servants join her, and he gives in (verse 23). She kills a fattened calf, kneads flour and bakes bread without yeast. ‘She served it to Saul and his servants, and they ate. And that night they got up and left’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Samuel's words are not new. They repeat what he said in chapter 15 almost exactly: the kingdom torn from Saul's hand and given to his neighbor, because of Amalek. The prophet who anointed Saul now announces his death. God's word stands, even when it is spoken in the strangest of settings.

Saul's name sounds like the word asked. The people asked for a king, and Saul was the answer. Now he asks the LORD and hears nothing, then asks a medium. The king who began as Israel's request ends asking in vain.

The woman is not mocked. She shows Saul real kindness. The meal is a full act of hospitality: a fattened calf, and bread baked in haste without waiting for it to rise, the kind of meal a host prepared quickly for an honored guest. The calf was kept in the house itself, as animals often were, on the ground floor below the family's rooms.

The chapter ends in darkness: ‘And that night they got up and left.’ A condemned king eats a meal from a woman his own law had outlawed, and walks out into the night.
passages.later:
Chronicles gives its verdict on Saul's end: “So Saul died for his unfaithfulness to the LORD, because he did not keep the word of the LORD and even consulted a medium for guidance” (1 Chronicles 10:13).

The psalms show that faithful people too have cried out when God seemed silent: “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1).
passages.hard:
Saul says that God has turned away from him and no longer answers. What should a reader make of God's silence?

God speaks to his people in the ways he has chosen, and his silence can itself be a judgment. God's silence toward Saul came after years of Saul refusing to listen. He seeks knowledge by a forbidden route, and he gets only the same word he had refused to heed. The chapter warns against trying to force guidance from God by any means at hand.

Not every silence is a judgment. The psalms are full of faithful people who cried out to a God who seemed far away, and God kept their prayers in the Bible. Saul's story does not mean that everyone who feels unheard has been rejected.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: At the end, a woman Saul's law had banned set food before him and urged him to eat. Ask where you have met unexpected mercy from someone you thought was far from God. And ask what it means that Saul heard the truth that night and still walked out into the dark.
